5068               	; 	' HARRY STARTS ON FLOOR 2 AT THE WEST EDGE OF SCREEN 7, and that is as
5069               	; 	' far left as the clock allows. The research says "the second-floor
5070               	; 	' elevator door", which is screen 3, and it cannot be done:
5071               	; 	'
5072               	; 	'   spawn      escape     round
5073               	; 	'   screen 3   119.9 s    100 s   -- impossible
5074               	; 	'   screen 5   108.1 s    100 s   -- impossible
5075               	; 	'   screen 6   102.3 s    100 s   -- impossible
5076               	; 	'   screen 7    96.4 s    100 s   -- 3.6 s of room
5077               	; 	'
5078               	; 	' HE STARTS AT THE LIFT NOW, AND THAT COST HIM A SPEED CHANGE.
5079               	; 	'
5080               	; 	' His escape route ZIGZAGS -- east along floor 2 to its escalator, WEST
5081               	; 	' along floor 3 to that one, then east again along the roof to the door.
5082               	; 	' From the lift on screen 3 that is 5,120 px against the 4,208 he walked
5083               	; 	' from screen 7, so at his old 1.75 px a pass he needed 105 s of a 100 s
5084               	; 	' round: he could never escape at all, and one of the two loss conditions
5085               	; 	' would quietly have stopped existing. This block used to say exactly that
5086               	; 	' and conclude the lift was impossible. It was impossible AT THAT SPEED.
5087               	; 	'
5088               	; 	' AND QUARTER-PIXELS COULD NOT EXPRESS THE ANSWER. A quarter of a pixel
5089               	; 	' per pass is worth about TEN SECONDS of his route, so the two candidate
5090               	; 	' values straddled the buzzer with nothing in between:
5091               	; 	'
5092               	; 	'   2.00 px/pass   escapes at 102.4 s of a 100 s round   never escapes
5093               	; 	'   2.25 px/pass   escapes at  91.0 s                    nine seconds early
5094               	; 	'
5095               	; 	' Worse, 2.25 was not reachable at all: the accumulator below had two
5096               	; 	' drain steps and therefore a hard ceiling of 2 px a pass, so hsp4 = 9
5097               	; 	' silently delivered 2.00 and he fell two thirds of a screen short of his
5098               	; 	' own escape. See the accumulator comment for the full account.
5099               	; 	'
5100               	; 	' Sixteenths with three drains put the step at about 2.5 s instead of 10,
5101               	; 	' and hsp64 = 35 (2.1875 px/pass) lands him at 96.3 s of the 100 --
5102               	; 	' escaping as the timer expires, which is what was asked for.
5103               	; 	'
5104               	; 	' 35 AND NOT 34, AND THE DIFFERENCE IS THE PLAYER'S OWN SCREEN. Measured
5105               	; 	' in play at 34: standing on an ordinary screen he escaped with one timer
5106               	; 	' unit left, and standing on the ELEVATOR screen he ran out of clock --
5107               	; 	' same route, same constant, decided by where the player happened to be.
5108               	; 	' Everything that moves is paced per loop PASS while the clock is paced in
5109               	; 	' real FRAMES, so a busy screen slows Harry in real time and the clock does

5353               	;
5354               	; 	' ======================================================================
5355               	; 	' DRAWING THE STORE -- four blits, once per screen crossing
5356               	; 	' ======================================================================
5357               	; 	' This is the whole cost of the flip, and it is paid on a discrete event
5358               	; 	' rather than every frame. RallyX's pan repaints 576 chars every time the
5359               	; 	' camera moves one cell; this repaints 640 about once every two seconds
5360               	; 	' of running.
5361               	; 	' SPRITES OFF BEFORE THE BLIT, NOT AFTER IT. This routine WAITs between
5362               	; 	' bands -- one band a frame, because a burst of VDP writes past a few
5363               	; 	' dozen in one frame is silently dropped -- so painting the new screen
5364               	; 	' takes several frames, and for all of them the OLD screen's actors and
5365               	; 	' obstacles were still sitting on top of it. Following Harry through a
5366               	; 	' seam showed him and every cart from the floor he had just left,
5367               	; 	' standing on a shop that was assembling itself underneath them.
5368               	; 	'
5369               	; 	' They are put back by the normal draw on the same pass, so the crossing
5370               	; 	' reads as a cut rather than as a dissolve with ghosts in it.
5371               	; 	' EACH BAND IS FINISHED BEFORE THE FRAME IT IS DRAWN IN ENDS, and the
5372               	; 	' bands go TOP DOWN. Both halves of that matter.
5373               	; 	'
5374               	; 	' The blit paints the template -- shelves, pillars and all -- and the
5375               	; 	' radios and prizes then take out the fixtures they stand in. Those two
5376               	; 	' used to be four frames apart: all four bands blitted with a WAIT
5377               	; 	' between them, and only afterwards the clearing. So every screen change
5378               	; 	' showed its counters and beams for several frames and then erased them,
5379               	; 	' which reads as the shop flickering rather than as it being drawn.
5380               	; 	'
5381               	; 	' TOP DOWN because a band's beam tops are stamped into the SLAB ROW OF
5382               	; 	' THE BAND ABOVE. Going bottom-up, band 1's blit would paint over the
5383               	; 	' beam tops band 0 had just put there. Going top-down the band above is
5384               	; 	' always already drawn, so everything a band needs -- its own cells and
5385               	; 	' the row it borrows overhead -- is final by the time its WAIT arrives.
5386               	; 	'
5387               	; 	' `3 - dq` rather than `FOR dlv = 3 TO 0 STEP -1`: dlv is an unsigned
5388               	; 	' byte, so counting down past zero wraps to 255 and the loop never ends
5389               	; 	' (CLAUDE.md 3A).

5468               	; 		#if NES
5469               	; 		#ddst = #ddst + 96		' three rows down -- see the overscan note
5470               	; 		' ONE ROW A FRAME, AND THIS IS WHY THREE BANDS IN FOUR LOST THEIR
5471               	; 		' LAST TWO ROWS. The NMI copies PPUBUF into the PPU during vblank
5472               	; 		' and its copy loop DOES NOT STOP WHEN VBLANK ENDS -- it runs to
5473               	; 		' the end of the descriptor whatever the raster is doing, and a
5474               	; 		' PPUDATA write outside vblank is discarded by the hardware.
5475               	; 		'
5476               	; 		' NTSC gives about 2273 CPU cycles of vblank, OAM DMA takes 513 of
5477               	; 		' them, and the copy costs roughly 14 a byte: about a hundred bytes
5478               	; 		' get through. A 32x5 band is 160, so the last sixty-odd vanished
5479               	; 		' -- three whole rows arrived, the fourth stopped eight or nine
5480               	; 		' cells in, and the floor bar and the air row above it were simply
5481               	; 		' never there. Measured on screen as `#########.......`, on every
5482               	; 		' band whose blit did not happen to start early.
5483               	; 		'
5484               	; 		' A row is 32 bytes, which fits with room to spare. This costs four
5485               	; 		' extra frames per band at round start and nothing during play.
5486               	; 		SCREEN stor_tpl,#dsrc,#ddst,32,3,32
5487               	; 		WAIT
5488               	; 		#dsrc = #dsrc + 96
5489               	; 		#ddst = #ddst + 96
5490               	; 		SCREEN stor_tpl,#dsrc,#ddst,32,2,32
5491               	; 		WAIT
5492               	; 		#else
5493               	; 		SCREEN stor_tpl,#dsrc,#ddst,32,5,32

6338               	; 			' THE BALL IS ON THE GROUND WHEN HE GETS TO IT.
6339               	; 			'
6340               	; 			' The bounce phase used to be `lx AND 31` -- a byte out of
6341               	; 			' the placement table, which is to say arbitrary. Run onto
6342               	; 			' a screen and the first ball might be at the bottom of its
6343               	; 			' arc, where a jump clears it, or at the top, where it has
6344               	; 			' to be ducked, and nothing on the way in told you which.
6345               	; 			' Sometimes you could keep running and jump it; sometimes
6346               	; 			' the same approach at the same speed could not be jumped

6348               	; 			'
6349               	; 			' So the phase is worked BACKWARDS from the meeting. He
6350               	; 			' closes 4 px a pass and the ball 2, so they meet in
6351               	; 			' (gap / 6) passes; the phase advances one a pass and wraps
6352               	; 			' at 32, so seeding it with the NEGATIVE of that lands it on
6353               	; 			' phase 0 -- the ground -- exactly as they arrive.
6354               	; 			'

6356               	; 			' wall and the ball starts `stag` in from the other, so it
6357               	; 			' is 232 - stag whichever direction the floor runs.

6553               	; 		' Past the two table slots the band has one more, at 8+llv, and
6554               	; 		' it is A RADIO OR NOTHING. Its kind does NOT come from the
6555               	; 		' table: the two bytes for slot 2 are still there and still
6556               	; 		' skipped, so the six-byte stride and every placement in
6557               	; 		' store.bas are untouched.

6560               	; 		' third radio appears only where that band already has radios,
6561               	; 		' which is what "a floor carries one, two or three of them"
6562               	; 		' means. Reading a kind out of the table here would have let a
6563               	; 		' third BALL through, and a third ball is a fifth sprite on the
6564               	; 		' scanline, the one thing the two-slot cap exists to prevent.

6570               	; 		' ONLY THE FIELDS THAT ARE EVER READ BACK are written. obd, obh,
6571               	; 		' obp and obc are write-only at 8-11 -- draw_obst and the
6572               	; 		' obstacle update both stop at 7, and coll_obst reads obh only
6573               	; 		' for a BALL, which this slot can never hold. obht IS read: it

8773               	;
8774               	; 	' THE VICTROLA, AS CHARACTERS. It never moves, so a sprite spent a
8775               	; 	' scan-line slot on something that can be painted once when the screen is
8776               	; 	' drawn -- and at one 16x16 sprite it could only ever be one colour and
8777               	; 	' one size. Four cells is twice the area for no sprite at all.
8778               	; 	'
8779               	; 	' It stands ON the slab, so it fills the band's rows 2 and 3; row 4 is
8780               	; 	' the floor bar itself -- and a PRIZE uses those same two rows.
8781               	; 	'
8782               	; 	' THEY CAN SHARE A BAND, AND THE CLAIM THAT USED TO BE HERE WAS WRONG.
8783               	; 	' It said the two never share a screen because "genstore keeps prizes off
8784               	; 	' the screens that carry hazards". That stopped being true the moment
8785               	; 	' hazard placement moved into the per-Krook stor_lvl table, and nothing
8786               	; 	' noticed, because the prize table is not part of the level table and
8787               	; 	' every check was written about one object at a time. Two money bags ended
8788               	; 	' up standing on a radio -- not fighting it, since the two routines poke
8789               	; 	' different cells and the later writer simply wins, so they read as one
8790               	; 	' merged object.
8791               	; 	'
8792               	; 	' WHAT KEEPS THEM APART IS COLUMNS. A radio stands at column 7, 15 or 23
8793               	; 	' (see lrc below); genstore's _off_the_rack nudges a prize clear of all
8794               	; 	' three, and checklevels.py reads that arithmetic back out of THIS file
8795               	; 	' and fails the build on any overlap.
8796               	; 	'
8797               	; 	' rdall = 1 paints all four cells, 0 repaints only the top-right one --
8798               	; 	' the pulse. Same address arithmetic either way, so the two cannot drift.
8799               	; 	' A BEAM TOP HANGS OUT OF THE FLOOR ABOVE, and the beam it belongs to has
8800               	; 	' just been taken away. `beam_tops` stamps SLABP -- the floor bar with the
8801               	; 	' support carried up through its lower three pixel rows -- into the slab
8802               	; 	' row above every pillar, and it runs BEFORE the radios and prizes are
8803               	; 	' placed. Clearing a pillar's own cells therefore left three grey pixels
8804               	; 	' dangling from the ceiling with nothing under them.
8805               	; 	'
8806               	; 	' TESTED, NOT ASSUMED: only SLABP is put back to SLAB. The row above the
8807               	; 	' top shopping floor is the ROOF DECK, a different character altogether,
8808               	; 	' and writing a floor bar over it would punch a hole in the roof.
8809               	; 	' A SHELF RUN IS FIVE CELLS WIDE and a radio covers two, so one standing
8810               	; 	' on a counter punched a hole through its middle and left the ends either
8811               	; 	' side -- the same incoherence the dangling pillar had, and worse, because
8812               	; 	' a counter reads as one object. The whole unit goes: walk outward along
8813               	; 	' the band's row 2 while the cell is still a shelf top, clearing it and
8814               	; 	' its bottom half together.
8815               	; 	'
8816               	; 	' Bounded at eight steps. The runs are five, so eight is slack rather
8817               	; 	' than a guess -- and an unbounded walk would run off the end of the row
8818               	; 	' if the name table ever held something unexpected.
8819               	; 	#if NES
8820               	; 	' WHAT THE TEMPLATE PUT IN THIS CELL, for a target that cannot read its
8821               	; 	' own video memory back. #nta is the offset INSIDE the band (0-159) and
8822               	; 	' nbl is the band; the answer is the byte SCREEN blitted there.
8823               	; 	'
8824               	; 	' This is the same arithmetic the blit itself does in draw_band --
8825               	; 	' template id out of stor_ix for (band, screen), times 160, plus the
8826               	; 	' offset -- so the two cannot disagree about what is on screen. It is
8827               	; 	' reading what the cell MEANS, not guessing from where the cell is: a
8828               	; 	' coordinate is a fact about this layout, the character is a fact about
8829               	; 	' the world, and only the second is safe to erase on.
8830               	; 	' SIXTEEN PATTERNS INTO THE BORROWED SLOTS, ONE VBLANK EACH.
8831               	; 	'
8832               	; 	' This is what esc_stand and esc_run cost on this machine. Four sprites is
8833               	; 	' 16 patterns and **a tile here is SIXTEEN bytes** -- two bitplanes -- so
8834               	; 	' the swap is 256 bytes. Three ways to spend that, and only one works:
8835               	; 	'
8836               	; 	'   nes_def         rendering off, ~2 frames of DARK SCREEN every mount.
8837               	; 	'                   This is the flash that was reported for three sessions.
8838               	; 	'   resident art    no upload at all -- but it needs 16 free patterns per
8839               	; 	'                   facing and there are only twelve free in the whole
8840               	; 	'                   table. Tried, and it overwrote Harry's left-facing legs.
8841               	; 	'   queued, chunked <- this. 64 bytes a vblank, four vblanks, picture up
8842               	; 	'                   the whole time.
8843               	; 	'
8844               	; 	' FOUR CHUNKS BECAUSE ONE WILL NOT FIT. The NMI's copy loop runs to the end
8845               	; 	' of its descriptor whatever the raster is doing, and the PPUADDR/PPUSCROLL
8846               	; 	' restore that follows it re-points the PPU mid-frame if it runs late --
8847               	; 	' which is the whole picture jumping for a frame. About 1679 cycles are
8848               	; 	' available after OAM DMA and a copy costs 50 + 14 a byte, so 64 bytes
8849               	; 	' (946) is comfortable and 256 (3634) is not. The WAITs are load-bearing:
8850               	; 	' PPUBUF accumulates for a whole pass, so without them all four descriptors
8851               	; 	' would flush in one vblank and cost exactly what the single call did.
8852               	; 	' checkvblank.py sums the descriptors BETWEEN WAITs for this reason.
8853               	; 	'
8854               	; 	' The cost is four frames at a mount or a dismount, once each, against two
8855               	; 	' frames of black. The caller sets #nsrc; nes_chrinit copies nchr, ncnt,
8856               	; 	' #ncol and nink into zero page rather than consuming the variables, so
8857               	; 	' they only need setting once.
8858               	; 	'
8859               	; 	' THE INTERMEDIATE STATE IS VISIBLE and that is accepted: for a frame or
8860               	; 	' two Harry is part standing and part running. He is stepping onto a
8861               	; 	' staircase at the time, which is exactly when a limb changing shape reads
8862               	; 	' as him changing pose.
8863               	; nes_swp16:
8864               	; 	' HARRY COMES OFF THE SCREEN FIRST, because this takes four frames.
8865               	; 	'
8866               	; 	' The swap is 256 bytes and a vblank carries about a hundred, so it goes as
8867               	; 	' four queued chunks with a WAIT between them (see below). The game loop is
8868               	; 	' stopped for those frames but the PPU is not, so whatever is half-written
8869               	; 	' is on screen: for a frame or two Harry was part standing and part
8870               	; 	' running -- reported as a glitch when he steps off a flight, and it is
8871               	; 	' one. All four of his sprites differ between the two poses, so there is no
8872               	; 	' ordering of the chunks that stays coherent.
8873               	; 	'
8874               	; 	' He is hidden instead. Four frames of absence at the exact moment he steps
8875               	; 	' on or off a staircase reads as nothing at all, where a figure assembled
8876               	; 	' out of two poses reads as a fault. draw_actors puts him back on its next
8877               	; 	' pass -- no flag to clear, because it writes all four slots every time.
8878               	; 	'
8879               	; 	' AND THE OAM MIRRORS WITH HIM. nes_oam2 copies slots 0-27 into 28-55 to
8880               	; 	' make each 16x16 actor two NES sprites, and it only runs at the end of
8881               	; 	' draw_actors -- which is not running during these WAITs. Without the call
8882               	; 	' below his left half would vanish and his RIGHT half would stay, which is
8883               	; 	' a worse artefact than the one being fixed.
8884               	; 	SPRITE 4,SPRHID,0,0,0
8885               	; 	SPRITE 5,SPRHID,0,0,0
8886               	; 	SPRITE 6,SPRHID,0,0,0
8887               	; 	SPRITE 7,SPRHID,0,0,0
8888               	; 	ASM JSR nes_oam2
8889               	; 	ASM JSR nes_suitcases
8890               	; 	nchr = P_HSTB
8891               	; 	ntab = 0
8892               	; 	#ncol = 0
8893               	; 	nink = 1
8894               	; 	ncnt = 4
8895               	; 	WAIT
8896               	; 	GOSUB nes_escd
8897               	; 	#nsrc = #nsrc + 32		' four patterns of source art, 8 bytes each
8898               	; 	nchr = nchr + 4
8899               	; 	WAIT
8900               	; 	GOSUB nes_escd
8901               	; 	#nsrc = #nsrc + 32
8902               	; 	nchr = nchr + 4
8903               	; 	WAIT
8904               	; 	GOSUB nes_escd
8905               	; 	#nsrc = #nsrc + 32
8906               	; 	nchr = nchr + 4
8907               	; 	WAIT
8908               	; 	GOSUB nes_escd
8909               	; 	RETURN
8910               	;
8911               	; nes_def_raw:
8912               	; 	' Setup only, just like nes_def; never called from the play loop.
8913               	; 	ASM JSR nes_chrraw
8914               	; 	RETURN
8915               	;
8916               	; nes_def:
8917               	; 	' WHAT DEFINE WOULD HAVE DONE. CVBasic implements no DEFINE at all for the
8918               	; 	' NES, on the reading that patterns live in cartridge CHR ROM -- but an
8919               	; 	' iNES header with a CHR-bank count of ZERO asks for 8 KB of CHR-RAM
8920               	; 	' instead, and that is the header CVBasic emits whenever the program uses
8921               	; 	' no BITMAP/CHRROM statement. So the pattern table here is ordinary VRAM
8922               	; 	' and this is the write. assets/nes_chr.asm carries the routine and the
8923               	; 	' reasoning; the caller sets #nsrc, nchr, ncnt and ntab.
8924               	; 	ASM JSR nes_chrup
8925               	; 	RETURN
8926               	;
8927               	; 	' AND THE SAME THING WITHOUT LOSING A FRAME. nes_def turns rendering off
8928               	; 	' and waits for a vblank the NMI therefore never services, so the game's
8929               	; 	' own WAIT then waits for the one after -- about two frames a call. That
8930               	; 	' is free at setup and ruinous anywhere that runs repeatedly. It builds
8931               	; 	' the same bytes into `nesb` and hands the NMI a single copy descriptor
8932               	; 	' instead. See assets/nes_chr.asm.
8933               	; 	'
8934               	; 	' THE NAME IS HISTORICAL: it was written for esc_tick, which redefines six
8935               	; 	' characters EVERY PASS on the two escalator screens and ran visibly slow
8936               	; 	' on nes_def. Nothing about it is escalator-specific -- it takes the same
8937               	; 	' inputs as nes_def plus #nesb, and the title's marquee uses it too, where
8938               	; 	' nes_def was switching the picture off twice a step and reading as a
8939               	; 	' flashing title screen.
8940               	; 	'
8941               	; 	' #nesb must point at a buffer of at least ncnt*16 bytes and is set once
8942               	; 	' in init_tables, which runs before boot: and therefore before the title.
8943               	; nes_escd:
8944               	; 	ASM JSR nes_chrq
8945               	; 	RETURN
8946               	;
8947               	; nes_tpl:
8948               	; 	nti = lv8(nbl)

8954               	; 	#ntc = #ntc + #sttp
8955               	; 	ntv = PEEK(#ntc)
8956               	; 	RETURN
8957               	; 	#endif

9042               	; 	' things. SLABP is the top of a free-standing pillar: a radio or a prize
9043               	; 	' stands in front of the pillar, so leaving its cap up there hangs a grey
9044               	; 	' stub over the fixture and that is what this routine exists to remove.
9045               	; 	' SLABE and ROOFSE are written ONLY at column 0 and column 31 -- read
9046               	; 	' beam_one, they are the two edge cases -- and there they are the
9047               	; 	' BUILDING'S OUTSIDE WALL, carrying its brick bond up through the floor
9048               	; 	' above. Clearing those took the support out from under the storey above
9049               	; 	' at the very edge of the screen, so the second floor visibly rested on
9050               	; 	' nothing.
9051               	; 	'
9052               	; 	' It could only ever show on the ESCALATOR screens, which is exactly how
9053               	; 	' it was reported -- one side, then mirrored on the other. The flight
9054               	; 	' fills the middle of an escalator band, so that screen's radio or prize
9055               	; 	' is pushed right out against the end wall; on every other screen no
9056               	; 	' fixture sits close enough for the two-cell clear at #bca and #bca+1 to

9059               cvb_BEAM_CLEAR
9060               	; 	' A BEAM TOP IS NOT IN THE TEMPLATE. beam_one VPOKEs it into the row
9061               	; 	' ABOVE each band, out of the pillar-column table -- so on the NES this
9062               	; 	' asks that same table rather than the PPU, and #bca sits one row above
9063               	; 	' the band, which is why it cannot go through nes_tpl.
9064               	; 	'
9065               	; 	' IT ALSO REPRODUCES beam_one'S EXCLUSION OF COLUMNS 0 AND 31. Those
9066               	; 	' carry SLABE/ROOFSE, the building's OUTSIDE WALL, not a pillar cap --
9067               	; 	' and clearing structure because an erase routine could not tell the

9708               	; 	' ONE ACCUMULATOR PER KIND, NOT PER SLOT. Every hazard of a kind moves at
9709               	; 	' that kind's speed, so three calls a pass serve all eight slots.
9710               	; 	'
9711               	; 	' Per-slot would have meant up to eight calls of O(fdv) work every pass --
9712               	; 	' the positive feedback loop CLAUDE.md 3A warns about, where a slow pass is
9713               	; 	' made slower by the very code meant to take the loop rate out of the

9749               	; 	' THE BOUNCE PHASE, ON THE SAME CLOCK AS THE JUMP AND AT ITS OLD PERIOD.
9750               	; 	'
9751               	; 	' The jump has always advanced by the frame delta (`kjf = kjf + fdv`) while
9752               	; 	' the bounce advanced once per PASS -- so whether a jump cleared a ball
9753               	; 	' depended on how busy the screen was, and the frame-by-frame property
9754               	; 	' checkball.py proves was exact only at fdv = 1.
9755               	; 	'
9756               	; 	' Stepping the phase by fdv directly would fix the clock and wreck the
9757               	; 	' game: a 32-phase arc would drop from about 1.35 s to 0.55 s, balls
9758               	; 	' bouncing 2.4x faster everywhere. So it gets a fraction of its own --
9759               	; 	' 25/64 of a phase per frame is 23.4 phases a second, against the 23.8 it
9760               	; 	' runs at today. Same bounce, now the same clock as the thing that has to
9761               	; 	' clear it.
9762               	; 	pacc = obac

10006               	;
10007               	; 	' ONE STEP OF A FRACTIONAL SPEED, FOR WHOEVER IS MOVING.
10008               	; 	'
10009               	; 	' `pacc` in and out, `psp64` in (sixty-fourths of a pixel per FRAME),
10010               	; 	' `pspd` out (whole pixels this pass). CVBasic has no locals, so the caller
10011               	; 	' stages its own accumulator in and takes it back out; that costs four
10012               	; 	' statements against the fourteen this used to be, written out per actor.
10013               	; 	'
10014               	; 	' Harry had the only copy. Kelly, the hazards and the bounce phase all need
10015               	; 	' the same thing -- everything the round clock judges has to advance by
10016               	; 	' ELAPSED FRAMES, or the loop rate becomes a difficulty dial and where the
10017               	; 	' player stands decides the outcome (DESIGN.md 0f-ter).
10018               	; 	'
10019               	; 	' TWO DRAINS CAP THE STEP AT 2 PER FRAME whatever psp64 says (CLAUDE.md
10020               	; 	' 3A: N drains cap the speed at N, and the surplus leaks into a byte that
10021               	; 	' wraps). Every caller is under that: Kelly 102/64 = 1.6, the fastest
10022               	; 	' hazard 76/64 = 1.2, Harry 57/64 = 0.9, the bounce phase 25/64 = 0.4.
10023               	; 	'
10024               	; 	' FIVE FRAMES, AND THREE WAS TOO FEW. At 2 px a frame five frames is 10 px,
10025               	; 	' and to skip a position window an actor must start outside it on one side
10026               	; 	' and land outside on the other, which needs 12. Three was the original bug
10027               	; 	' in miniature: the lift screen runs at almost exactly 20 passes a second,
10028               	; 	' which IS fdv = 3, so every hitch there lost a frame. The clamp exists for
10029               	; 	' a genuine stall and at five it only fires for one.

10518               	; 	' THE SIXTEENTH-PIXEL ACCUMULATOR. hx is one unsigned byte per screen
10519               	; 	' (2), so there is nowhere to keep a fraction -- the fraction lives here
10520               	; 	' and is spent as whole pixels. THREE IFs, not a loop and not a divide:
10521               	; 	' `%` and `/` both compile to a real TMS9900 DIV (CLAUDE.md 3A) and this
10522               	; 	' runs every pass.
10523               	; 	'
10524               	; 	' THE NUMBER OF DRAINS IS A CEILING ON THE SPEED, AND THAT IS THE WHOLE
10525               	; 	' POINT OF THIS COMMENT. Each IF can spend one whole pixel, so N drains
10526               	; 	' cap hspd at N px per pass NO MATTER WHAT hsp64 SAYS. The invariant is:
10527               	; 	'
10528               	; 	'     hacc is under 16 on entry, and hsp64 is at most 48,
10529               	; 	'     so hacc is under 64 here and three drains always suffice.
10530               	; 	'
10531               	; 	' KEEP hsp64 <= 48. This was quarter-pixels with TWO drains and the same
10532               	; 	' invariant written the same way -- "hsp4 is at most 8, so it can never
10533               	; 	' need a third" -- and it was correct until somebody set hsp4 = 9 without
10534               	; 	' re-reading it. The crook then ran at a flat 2.0 px/pass while every
10535               	; 	' comment, the design table and assets/checkchase.py all said 2.25, and
10536               	; 	' the surplus quarter leaked into hacc and wrapped the byte every 256
10537               	; 	' passes. Nothing failed; he simply arrived two thirds of a screen short
10538               	; 	' of his own escape. checkchase.py now counts these IFs and refuses a
10539               	; 	' speed the drains cannot deliver.
10540               	; 	'
10541               	; 	' 7, NOT 6, AND THE REASON IS MEASURED. Tracked off the reference video
10542               	; 	' (DESIGN.md 4a), the 2600's Kelly covers 0.40 screen widths a second and
10543               	; 	' its Harry 0.193 -- a ratio of 2.07. At hsp4 = 6 ours was 2.67, and the
10544               	; 	' crook visibly strolled. 7 brings it to 2.29. 8 would match the original
10545               	; 	' exactly and cannot be used: Kelly's route here is 1.95x Harry's, so a
10546               	; 	' speed ratio of 2.0 leaves the on-foot chase 0.2 s of slack, which is no

10647               cv566
10648               	;
10649               	; 	' HE WALKS BY REAL TIME, NOT BY LOOP PASS -- one accumulate-and-drain per
10650               	; 	' ELAPSED FRAME rather than per pass. Everything that moves here used to be
10651               	; 	' per pass while the CLOCK is paced by the frame delta, so a busy screen
10652               	; 	' slowed Harry in real seconds and the clock did not slow with him: the
10653               	; 	' same uninterrupted escape finished with nine timer units in hand from a
10654               	; 	' light screen and none at all from the lift screen, decided by where the
10655               	; 	' player happened to be standing. Now he covers the same ground per second
10656               	; 	' wherever anybody is (DESIGN.md 0f-ter).
10657               	; 	'
10658               	; 	' A LOOP, NOT A MULTIPLY. `*` compiles to a real TMS9900 MPY, and reading a
10659               	; 	' 16-bit variable straight after one returns the product's HIGH word
10660               	; 	' (CLAUDE.md 3A). fdv is 1..3 here, so this is at most three adds.
10661               	; 	'
10662               	; 	' SIXTY-FOURTHS, AND ONLY TWO DRAINS -- both fall out of accumulating per
10663               	; 	' FRAME instead of per pass. He covers under a pixel a frame, so two drains
10664               	; 	' are ample where the per-pass version needed three; and the finer unit is
10665               	; 	' what makes the speed tunable at all. In sixteenths one step was about six
10666               	; 	' SECONDS of his route, so nothing landed near the buzzer; in sixty-fourths
10667               	; 	' it is about one and a half. Keep hsp64 <= 128: hacc is under 64 on entry,
10668               	; 	' so 64 + 128 stays inside a byte and two drains always suffice.
10669               	; 	'
10670               	; 	' AND THE STEP IS CLAMPED TO THREE FRAMES' WORTH, WHICH IS NOT A DETAIL.
10671               	; 	' Two tests sample his position once a pass and neither interpolates:
10672               	; 	'
10673               	; 	'   ARRIVAL   `hdx < 6` around the escalator or the roof door -- an ELEVEN
10674               	; 	'             pixel window. A step over 10 px can jump clean across it and
10675               	; 	'             he never arrives at all.
10676               	; 	'   THE CATCH `hdd < CATCHR` is 12, a 23-wide band, and Kelly closes 4 of
10677               	; 	'             it himself -- so Harry over ~18 px could pass through the Kop
10678               	; 	'             between two passes without either sample being inside it.
10679               	; 	'
10680               	; 	' The clamp and the drains live in pace_step now, with the reasoning; the
10681               	; 	' numbers above are what sized them. Measured: TIME 02 on the lift screen
10682               	; 	' against TIME 04 on a light one when the clamp was 3, and 00 against 09

11154               	;
11155               	; 	' ======================================================================
11156               	; 	' COLLISIONS -- pure arithmetic against RAM, no VDP reads
11157               	; 	' ======================================================================
11158               	; 	' Kelly's box is [kfh, kfh + kh) above the slab; an obstacle's is
11159               	; 	' [ohb, oht). The ball's inset hitbox is what makes 8..10 avoidable both
11160               	; 	' ways -- without it there is a height at which the ball can be neither
11161               	; 	' jumped nor ducked, and an unavoidable hazard is not difficulty.
11162               	; 	' ONE HIT PER CONTACT, WITH A REFRACTORY PERIOD.
11163               	; 	'
11164               	; 	' The overlap test is true on every frame the player is touching
11165               	; 	' something, so with no latch at all one clumsy cart charges nine seconds
11166               	; 	' several times over -- and what the player sees is the clock jumping by
11167               	; 	' 27, from which the only available conclusion is that the penalty is
11168               	; 	' broken.
11169               	; 	'
11170               	; 	' A latch that clears on the first non-overlapping frame is still not
11171               	; 	' enough, and the case that breaks it is the BOUNCING BALL: it rises off
11172               	; 	' the player between bounces, which is a genuine loss of contact, so a
11173               	; 	' player standing still under one is taxed on every single bounce while
11174               	; 	' being given no opportunity to do anything about it. Technically two
11175               	; 	' collisions; in play, one situation.
11176               	; 	'
11177               	; 	' So obht() is a countdown, not a flag. A hit sets it to HITREF; it ticks
11178               	; 	' down only while the player is CLEAR, and the same obstacle cannot charge
11179               	; 	' again until it reaches zero. Contact holds the count up, so parking
11180               	; 	' inside something never earns a second penalty either.
11181               	; coll_obst:
11182               cvb_COLL_OBST

11548               	; 	' THE FLOOR CLEARS WHEN YOU ARE HIT, and stays clear until you re-enter
11549               	; 	' the screen. Nine seconds is a heavy penalty on a fifty-unit clock, and
11550               	; 	' taking it while still standing among the things that charged it -- with
11551               	; 	' a second hazard 48 px behind the first -- is how one mistake becomes
11552               	; 	' three. Clearing the row makes the penalty a single event you can walk
11553               	; 	' away from.
11554               	; 	'
11555               	; 	' BOTH SLOTS, WHATEVER IS IN THEM. Radios used to be exempt: they are
11556               	; 	' CHARACTERS stamped into the name table rather than sprites, so zeroing
11557               	; 	' the kind would have stopped them colliding while leaving them plainly
11558               	; 	' visible on the shelf, and a fixture that is still there has to still be
11559               	; 	' there. That was a reason to UNDRAW them, not a reason to keep them --
11560               	; 	' and it left the one hazard that cannot leave on its own as the only one
11561               	; 	' the mercy did not cover. haz_off now takes the characters with it.
11562               	; 	'

11564               	; 	' template, and it runs only on a seam crossing or a round start, so

11566               	; 	' come back and the hazards are simply placed again.

11737               	; 	' AND THEY HAVE TO BE AT THE SAME HEIGHT, NOT MERELY ON THE SAME FLOOR.
11738               	; 	'
11739               	; 	' `hlv` does not change until a ride ENDS -- a crook stepping onto a
11740               	; 	' flight keeps the floor he left until he arrives at the next one. So
11741               	; 	' while he was most of a storey up or down the stairs he still counted as
11742               	; 	' standing on the floor he started from, and a Kop who ran over the head
11743               	; 	' of the flight arrested him through the floor. Reported from play:
11744               	; 	' "I run over top of him, even though we do not touch".
11745               	; 	'
11746               	; 	' It is the same shape of bug as the catch that fired at MAXIMUM
11747               	; 	' separation: a test that is right about one axis and silent about the
11748               	; 	' other, where the silent one happens to be true nearly all the time.
11749               	; 	'
11750               	; 	' UNSIGNED-SAFE. Riding up is above the shared floor and riding down is
11751               	; 	' below it, which is a signed quantity, and CVBasic's variables are not.
11752               	; 	' So both are collected as POSITIVE heights on opposite sides -- Kelly's
11753               	; 	' climb plus Harry's descent on one side, Harry's climb on the other --
11754               	; 	' and the difference is taken between two numbers that cannot go
11755               	; 	' negative. Two riders passing on the same flight measure the sum of
11756               	; 	' their heights, which is exactly the distance between them.

12441               cv761
12442               	; 	' HE IS STRIPED FROM CAP TO HEM. Both stripe colours run the whole upper
12443               	; 	' half, so both boxes span rows 0-15 and neither can be tucked away --
12444               	; 	' affordable only because Kelly's hat moved into a box of its own. His
12445               	; 	' FACE is pushed DOWN instead (hy+3, box 3..18) so it clears the cap
12446               	; 	' rows, where his two stripe boxes plus Kelly's hat and face already
12447               	; 	' make four. Worst line of a meeting: exactly four, nothing dropped.
12448               	; 	' HE RISES A PIXEL ON THE RECOVERY BEATS. A runner is highest at mid-flight
12449               	; 	' and lowest at contact; with the body pinned at a constant y, alternating
12450               	; 	' legs under a motionless torso reads as a dance rather than as travel.
12451               	; 	'
12452               	; 	' One pixel is enough at this size, and it lifts the BODY ONLY -- the legs
12453               	; 	' keep their y, so the planted foot stays on the floor and the figure
12454               	; 	' stretches at the waist instead of hopping. Lifting the legs too would be
12455               	; 	' a jump.
12456               	; 	'
12457               	; 	' Beats 2 and 4 are the recoveries, which is exactly `hanim AND 8` -- the
12458               	; 	' cycle's LOW beat bit. IT MUST MOVE WITH THE BEAT BITS ABOVE IT: on the
12459               	; 	' wrong bit he rises and falls twice per stride, a second clock inside one
12460               	; 	' figure, which is the flapping of DESIGN.md 0j2 in the vertical.
12461               	; 	'
12462               	; 	' Safe because HARRY'S COLLISION HAS NO VERTICAL COMPONENT: he is caught on
12463               	; 	' `same level AND |dx| < CATCHR`. Doing this to Kelly would desynchronise
12464               	; 	' his sprite from the ball and biplane windows in DESIGN.md 5a, which is
12465               	; 	' why it is not done to him.
12466               	; 	' THE WHOLE FIGURE RISES, legs included, rather than the body stretching
12467               	; 	' away from the feet. Two reasons, and the second was not the first plan:
12468               	; 	'
12469               	; 	'   * It is what a run does. Mid-flight BOTH feet are off the ground, so
12470               	; 	'     lifting the legs with the body is the correct pose, not a compromise.
12471               	; 	'   * Lifting the body alone opens a one-pixel gap at the waist, and the
12472               	; 	'     torso's bottom row and the legs' top row do not align across it --
12473               	; 	'     green shows through and he reads as coming apart.
12474               	; 	'
12475               	; 	' It also keeps `hfy = hy - 7` and `hy2 = hy + 16` LITERAL, which is not a
12476               	; 	' cosmetic concern: assets/checkbands.py reads each band's draw offset by
12477               	; 	' parsing those exact expressions. Bobbing a differently-named variable
12478               	; 	' made them unreadable and the gate failed the build -- correctly. A
12479               	; 	' checker that can no longer see what it checks has to fail, not shrug.
12480               	; 	' THE RECOVERY LIFT IS A RUNNING THING. Standing on a step he would

12937               	; 	' THE SCANNER
12938               	; 	' ======================================================================
12939               	; 	' Rows 21-23, 16 chars wide, centred: 48 characters whose PATTERNS are
12940               	; 	' poked directly, so a moving dot costs two writes and no name-table
12941               	; 	' traffic. With the flip (DESIGN.md 2a) this is how you know where Harry
12942               	; 	' is at all -- he can be one pixel off-screen and completely invisible.
12943               	; 	'
12944               	; 	' Rows 21-23 all sit in the THIRD screen third, so every scanner pattern
12945               	; 	' is at base 4096 and no third-selection arithmetic is needed.
12946               	; 	'
12947               	; 	' BOTH DOTS ARE WHITE and Kelly's BLINKS. The manual wants Kelly black
12948               	; 	' and Harry white, but this is the TMS9918's two-colours-per-8x1-cell
12949               	; 	' mode: a black dot and a white dot on the same pixel row of the same
12950               	; 	' character cannot both exist. Blinking distinguishes them with one
12951               	; 	' colour, which is what RallyX does with its player dot.
12952               	; 	' THE STEPS MOVE, AND EVERY ESCALATOR ON SCREEN MOVES WITH THEM. A flight
12953               	; 	' is twelve characters -- six per direction, sliced out of a rendered
12954               	; 	' 64x40 bitmap by genart.py -- so rewriting those twelve PATTERNS animates
12955               	; 	' the lot: 96 bytes, no name-table traffic, and the same cost whether one
12956               	; 	' flight is visible or ten. The phases slide the cells ALONG the slope, so
12957               	; 	' the steps travel up the flight rather than drifting sideways.

12983               	; 	' ONE PHASE PER PASS, AND NEVER MORE. There are four phases covering an
12984               	; 	' 8 px period, so advancing by the frame delta ALIASES: at fdv 2 the
12985               	; 	' pattern flips between two positions half a period apart and the
12986               	; 	' direction stops being readable, and at fdv 3 the sequence runs 0,3,2,1
12987               	; 	' -- the staircase visibly runs BACKWARDS, carrying its steps down while
12988               	; 	' the rider goes up. That is the wagon-wheel effect, and no amount of
12989               	; 	' phase arithmetic fixes it: a 4-phase cycle can only be stepped by 1.
12990               	; 	'
12991               	; 	' So the ANIMATION is the clock here, and the rider is paced from it --
12992               	; 	' see move_kelly, which advances him by the same fixed 2-and-1 per pass
12993               	; 	' rather than by fdv. Locking the two together is the only way they
12994               	; 	' cannot drift, and it is what "the player moves at the rate the steps
12995               	; 	' carry him" actually means. The cost is that a ride takes 36 passes
12996               	; 	' rather than 36 frames, so it slows down when the loop does -- which is
12997               	; 	' the honest behaviour for a machine that is carrying you.

13011               	; 	#if NES
13012               	; 	' A VBLANK OF ITS OWN, AND THIS IS THE WHOLE-SCREEN FLASH.
13013               	; 	'
13014               	; 	' PPUBUF is not flushed when it is written -- it ACCUMULATES for the whole
13015               	; 	' pass and the NMI empties it in one go, so every VPOKE the radar makes,
13016               	; 	' every HUD digit and this upload all land in the SAME vblank. And the
13017               	; 	' handler's copy loop does not stop when vblank ends: it runs to the end of
13018               	; 	' the descriptor and then writes PPUADDR and both PPUSCROLLs, which
13019               	; 	' mid-frame re-points the PPU's own render address. The rest of that frame
13020               	; 	' is drawn from the wrong place. On screen that is not a dropped tile, it
13021               	; 	' is the ENTIRE PICTURE jumping for a frame -- which is what has been
13022               	; 	' reported, repeatedly, as the screen flashing on an escalator.
13023               	; 	'
13024               	; 	' The arithmetic says it cannot be anything else. NTSC vblank is about
13025               	; 	' 2273 CPU cycles; NMI entry, the flicker test and OAM DMA spend ~560 of
13026               	; 	' them before a single byte is copied. A copy descriptor costs ~50 cycles
13027               	; 	' plus 14 a byte, so these six characters -- 96 bytes, because a tile is
13028               	; 	' SIXTEEN bytes in two bitplanes, not eight -- are ~1400 on their own.
13029               	; 	' That leaves about 270 cycles, or SIX single-byte pokes, for everything
13030               	; 	' else the pass queued. The radar alone beats that whenever a dot moves.
13031               	; 	'
13032               	; 	' Nothing smaller fixes it, because the overrun is per FRAME, not per
13033               	; 	' second: slowing the animation down just makes the bad frames rarer.
13034               	; 	' Splitting the six characters across two frames tears the staircase, and
13035               	; 	' only three of the six have a constant second bitplane, so dropping a
13036               	; 	' plane does not buy a frame's worth either. What DOES work is giving the
13037               	; 	' upload a vblank with nothing else in it: this WAIT flushes the pass's
13038               	; 	' radar and HUD writes, and the descriptor queued below is then almost all
13039               	; 	' the next vblank has to carry -- ~1960 cycles of 2273, inside the window
13040               	; 	' with room to spare.
13041               	; 	'
13042               	; 	' IT COSTS ONE FRAME A PASS, on the two screens that carry a flight and
13043               	; 	' nowhere else -- esc_tick has already returned on the other six. The
13044               	; 	' rider is paced from the animation rather than from the frame delta (see
13045               	; 	' below), so a slower pass slows the ride too and the two cannot drift.
13046               	; 	WAIT
13047               	; 	#endif
13048               	; 	' ONLY THE CELLS THAT MOVE, AND ONLY THIS SCREEN'S. genart.py measures
13049               	; 	' which cells move -- the step cells and the COMPOSITE copies of them
13050               	; 	' that cross a floor -- and groups them WEST then EAST, because only one
13051               	; 	' direction is ever on screen: screen 0 carries a west flight and screen
13052               	; 	' 7 an east one.
13053               	; 	'
13054               	; 	' THIS IS THE ONLY PER-PASS WORK UNIQUE TO THESE TWO SCREENS, and it is
13055               	; 	' `define_char`, which in bitmap mode is LDIRVM3 -- the TRIPLE copy, once
13056               	; 	' per screen third. It therefore costs three times what the character
13057               	; 	' count suggests, which is why these screens run slower than the rest.
13058               	; 	'
13059               	; 	' THE WEST SCREEN USED TO COST HALF AS MUCH AGAIN, because it carries TWO
13060               	; 	' flights: floor 1's crosses into a shop floor and floor 3's into the
13061               	; 	' roof, so it needed both composite sets -- nine characters against the
13062               	; 	' east's six, 216 bytes a pass against 144. It measured 20 passes a
13063               	; 	' second where the east screen managed 24-26. The two sets are
13064               	; 	' PIXEL-IDENTICAL and are never wanted in the same screen THIRD, so they
13065               	; 	' share their characters now and are told apart by the per-third colour
13066               	; 	' table (see esc_deck_col in setup). Six either side.
13067               	; 	'
13068               	; 	' The handrail and the frame sit past the end of both ranges and never
13069               	; 	' move at all.
13070               	; 	IF klsc = 0 THEN

13398               	; 	' Without this the scanner is two dots in a void: you can see THAT Harry is

13407               	; 	'

13869               	;
13870               	; 	' Blank the canvas by WRITING zeros rather than copying 384 of them out
13871               	; 	' of ROM. This runs twice a game -- at setup and on a new Krook -- so a
13872               	; 	' loop costs nothing anybody can perceive, and it hands the fixed area
13873               	; 	' back the best part of half a kilobyte, which is the budget that
13874               	; 	' actually binds. Paced in bursts: a few hundred VDP writes in a single
13875               	; 	' frame are silently dropped (CLAUDE.md 3A).
13876               	; scan_wipe:
13877               cvb_SCAN_WIPE
13878               	; 	' THIS ADDRESS IS A CHARACTER CODE IN DISGUISE, AND IT WENT STALE.
13879               	; 	' 4096 is the pattern table's BOTTOM THIRD -- rows 16-23, which is
13880               	; 	' band 0 and the radar together -- and the canvas characters begin at
13881               	; 	' genart's SCAN_FIRST, so the base is 4096 + SCAN_FIRST*8. It was
13882               	; 	' written out by hand as 4096 + 160*8 when SCAN_FIRST was 160; art
13883               	; 	' added later moved SCAN_FIRST to 208 and nothing moved this with it,
13884               	; 	' so the wipe zeroed the 48 characters BELOW the canvas and never
13885               	; 	' touched the canvas at all.
13886               	; 	'
13887               	; 	' Two of those forty-eight are STRUCTURE. ENDWALL is the building's
13888               	; 	' outside wall and SLABP is a pillar's cap. Blanking a pattern in ONE
13889               	; 	' THIRD leaves a character that draws correctly everywhere else and
13890               	; 	' falls back to its own background colour here -- so the GROUND FLOOR's
13891               	; 	' outside wall turned into plain green while the identical wall one
13892               	; 	' storey up was perfect, and the ground floor's pillars lost the brick
13893               	; 	' carried up through the bar above them. ENDWALL appears only on
13894               	; 	' screens 0 and 7, which is exactly why it was reported as happening
13895               	; 	' only on the escalator screens, mirrored side to side.
13896               	; 	'
13897               	; 	' The name table was correct the whole time. Probing it said so, four
13898               	; 	' times. It was the GLYPH that was empty, in one third only -- which a
13899               	; 	' probe that copies the character somewhere else to look at it cannot
13900               	; 	' see, because the copy renders from a different third's pattern.
13901               	; 	'
13902               	; 	' renumber.py rewrites this line from genart.SCAN_FIRST, and
13903               	; 	' checkstruct.py fails the build if the two disagree.
13904               	; 	#swa = 5760			' 4096 + SCAN_FIRST*8, the canvas patterns
13905 E906 0200  20 	li r0,5760
     E908 1680     
13906 E90A C800  38 	mov r0,@cvb__SWA
     E90C 20E6     
13907               	; 	#if NES
13908               	; 	' AN NES TILE IS SIXTEEN BYTES, NOT EIGHT -- two bitplanes. DERIVED FROM
13909               	; 	' THE LINE ABOVE rather than written out again: renumber.py rewrites that
13910               	; 	' literal out of genart.SCAN_FIRST and checkstruct.py checks it, and a
13911               	; 	' second hand-kept copy of the same number is exactly the fault recorded
13912               	; 	' in the comment above this routine.
13913               	; 	#swa = #swa + #swa
13914               	; 	#swa = #swa - 4096
13915               	; 	#endif
13916               	; 	' THE SHADOW TAKES ITS BASE FROM THE LINE ABOVE, never from a second
13917               	; 	' copy of the number. renumber.py rewrites that literal out of
13918               	; 	' genart.SCAN_FIRST, and a hand-kept duplicate of it is precisely the
13919               	; 	' fault recorded in the comment above -- one copy moved, the other did
13920               	; 	' not, and the wipe spent months clearing the wrong forty-eight
13921               	; 	' characters. 6 x 64 is 384, which is the size of nsc.
13922               	; 	#if NES
13923               	; 	#nsb = #swa
13924               	; 	#nsi = 0
13925               	; 	#endif
13926               	; 	#if NES
13927               	; 	' TWELVE BURSTS, NOT SIX: 48 tiles of SIXTEEN bytes. The shadow is indexed
13928               	; 	' by the same offset the PPU address uses, so it grows with the stride --
13929               	; 	' half of what it holds is plane 1; black flights use it too.
13930               	; 	' AND THE CANVAS IS WIPED TO GREEN, NOT TO BLACK.
13931               	; 	'
13932               	; 	' On the TI a blank canvas is zeros and the COLOUR TABLE says what the
13933               	; 	' background is. There is no colour table here: a pixel's colour is its
13934               	; 	' two bitplane bits, so "green background" means plane 0 SET everywhere
13935               	; 	' and plane 1 clear -- index 1, which is the store's green in P0.
13936               	; 	'
13937               	; 	' THAT INVERTS THE SENSE OF EVERY FEATURE DRAWN ON TOP. The floor lines
13938               	; 	' add plane 1 to reach index 3 (gold), and the escalator diagonals CLEAR
13939               	; 	' plane 0 and SET plane 1 to reach index 2 (black); see scan_or1.
13940               	; 	' Writing zeros here instead would give the canvas the grey backdrop.
13941               	; 	'
13942               	; 	' A tile is sixteen bytes: 0-7 are plane 0 and 8-15 plane 1, so the byte's
13943               	; 	' position within its tile decides which it is.

15079               	;
15080               	; 	' THE BONUS IS COUNTED OUT, NOT AWARDED. Dropping the whole sum into the
15081               	; 	' score in one frame tells the player a number; ticking the clock down a
15082               	; 	' unit at a time, with the score climbing and a beat under each step,
15083               	; 	' tells them what the number was FOR. It is the pay-off for every second
15084               	; 	' they saved, and every arcade game of this era spends a moment on it.
15085               	; 	'
15086               	; 	' It also costs nothing to get right: the loop already has to run down
15087               	; 	' `tsec`, so the animation IS the calculation, and the repeated-addition
15088               	; 	' note below stops applying -- each step adds one band's worth.
15089               	; 	'
15090               	; 	' x100 for Krooks 1-9, x200 for 10-15, x300 from 16. Two independent
15091               	; 	' sources agree on those bands; the manual's own wording suggests
15092               	; 	' 1-8 / 9-16 / 17+ and DESIGN.md 0 records the disagreement.
15093               	; 	'
15094               	; 	' IN UNITS OF TEN, WHICH IS WHAT THE SCORE IS COUNTED IN, so the bands are
15095               	; 	' 10 / 20 / 30 and not 100 / 200 / 300.
15096               	; 	'
15097               	; 	' They were 100 / 200 / 300 and paid TEN TIMES the right bonus -- 1,000 a
15098               	; 	' time unit where the original pays 100. `add_score` takes `#addv` in units

15229               	;
15230               	; 	' AND IT ENDS ON ITS LAST BLIP -- there is no closing accent.
15231               	; 	'
15232               	; 	' Two were tried. The bench's own ending for this variant rose a fourth,
15233               	; 	' to 2,542 Hz, and a square wave there is a shriek -- the same fault the
15234               	; 	' pickup was rewritten for. Dropping it an OCTAVE BELOW the ticks, to
15235               	; 	' 518 Hz, was reported the same way, and that one cannot be too high by
15236               	; 	' any measure: it is the lowest note in the effect.
15237               	; 	'
15238               	; 	' So the complaint is not the pitch, it is the extra note. A tally is
15239               	; 	' arithmetic, and arithmetic finishes when the last term is added; a
15240               	; 	' flourish after it is a second event the player has to interpret, and
15241               	; 	' the HUD has already said the clock is empty. The count stops when the
15242               	; 	' counting stops.
15243               	;
15244               	; 	' `calc_bonus` USED TO LIVE HERE and computed the whole sum by repeated
15245               	; 	' addition, to dodge two hazards at once: `tsec * bmul` is an 8-bit
15246               	; 	' product (a 50-unit capture in the x300 band pays 15,000, six times past
15247               	; 	' a byte), and multiplying properly lands on the MPY/r0 hazard where a
15248               	; 	' 16-bit variable read straight after being multiplied returns the
15249               	; 	' product's high word. Counting the bonus out a unit at a time (above)
15250               	; 	' removes the multiply entirely rather than working around it -- the loop
15251               	; 	' the player watches IS the arithmetic.
15252               	; 	'
15253               	; 	' It also fixed the last-tick case for free: `bn_loop` tests `tsec = 0`
15254               	; 	' on entry, where the old `FOR bi = 1 TO tsec` would have run its body
15255               	; 	' once and paid a full multiplier for no time at all (CLAUDE.md 3A).

15303               	; 	' thing that had just hit him vanished and the sound played over an empty
15304               	; 	' store. The hit that ENDS a round is the worst case: `do_hit` sets tout
15305               	; 	' before the freeze starts and the main loop leaves on the very next pass,

15314               	; 	' the store being deleted and then two words on an empty field -- which
15315               	; 	' reads as the program ending rather than as the game ending. The store
15316               	; 	' stays; the message sits in the middle of it.

15320               	; 	' row above and below the text is a frame for the price of two strings and

15601               	;
15602               	; 	' A SOUND STILL PLAYING WHEN THE ROUND ENDS IS ALLOWED TO FINISH.
15603               	; 	'
15604               	; 	' This used to open with a bare `GOSUB snd_off`, which cut it dead. That
15605               	; 	' was not an accident: the decay counters are ticked by the MAIN LOOP, and
15606               	; 	' this pause REPLACES the main loop, so a tone left latched with nothing
15607               	; 	' ticking it hangs for the full ninety frames -- the sticky-audio failure
15608               	; 	' this game has already shipped twice. The answer is to DRAIN the counters
15609               	; 	' rather than to stop silencing.
15610               	; 	'
15611               	; 	' CLEAR THE PENDING LATCHES FIRST. sf* flags are sounds that have not
15612               	; 	' happened yet; left set, the drain below would START one and the pause
15613               	; 	' would end with a fresh note ringing into the next round.
15614               	; 	'
15615               	; 	' THEN TICK sfx_tick WHOLE, not some decay-only part of it. The five
15616               	; 	' counters do not all live in one place: sot, sht and spt are a block at
15617               	; 	' the tail, but spz (the prize arpeggio) and swt (the jump warble) tick up
15618               	; 	' among the code that starts sounds. Draining only the tail would finish a
15619               	; 	' footstep and still cut the arpeggio, which is the one effect with a
15620               	; 	' phrase worth saving. Calling the whole routine also leaves the write
15621               	; 	' order on CHANNEL 2 alone, which spz and spt share.
15622               	; 	'
15623               	; 	' EVERY THIRD FRAME, because the main loop runs about 2.5 frames per pass
15624               	; 	' and this loop waits one frame per turn. Ticking every frame would play
15625               	; 	' everything at two and a half times its tuned speed. Three frames a tick
15626               	; 	' is ~17% slow and gives 30 ticks against the longest effect's 20 passes.
15627               	; 	'
15628               	; 	' THE LOOP COUNTS TICKS, NOT FRAMES, which is what makes the pacing free.
15629               	; 	' Counting 91 frames and firing on every third needs a second counter, an
15630               	; 	' increment and a test -- 48 bytes, on a fixed area with 66 left. Counting
15631               	; 	' 31 TICKS of three WAITs each is the same 93 frames and the same three
15632               	; 	' frames per tick, with none of that. The duration changes by two frames.
15633               	; 	'
15634               	; 	' snd_off still runs at the END, as the backstop for anything the drain
15635               	; 	' did not finish.
15636               	; pause_beat:
15637               cvb_PAUSE_BEAT
15638               	; 	GOSUB snd_pend
15639 F150 06A0  32 	bl @jsr
     F152 A980

15644               	; 	' call sites would have cost code to say the same thing worse.
15645               	; 	'
15646               	; 	' THE LOOP COUNT AND NOT THE WAITS. sfx_tick runs once per pass, so it

15648               	; 	' decay counters are in frames and every effect would ring twice as long.

16062               	;
16063               	; 	' THE LOW-TIME WARNING IS SILENT. There was a beep a second under ten, and
16064               	; 	' it was the wrong instrument for the job: the last ten seconds are the
16065               	; 	' busiest part of a round, so a repeating tone arrives exactly when the
16066               	; 	' player most needs to hear the hazards, and it fought the prize arpeggio
16067               	; 	' for channel 2 as well. The flash says the same thing and says it in the
16068               	; 	' place the player is already looking.
16069               	;
16070               	; 	' FOOTSTEPS ARE NOISE, AND ON THE NOISE CHANNEL -- testsounds variant A.
16071               	; 	'
16072               	; 	' They were two alternating TONES on channel 0, which is neither what the
16073               	; 	' original does nor a good use of a channel: the recording says a footstep
16074               	; 	' is a short burst of white noise, and channel 3 was sitting unused while
16075               	; 	' the footsteps and the jump sweep shared channel 0 and had to take turns.
16076               	; 	'
16077               	; 	' TESTSOUNDS RUN D: a SHORT tick at the measured RATE.
16078               	; 	'
16079               	; 	' The two dials are independent and both were tried at the bench. The
16080               	; 	' 2600 plays a 64 ms burst every 165 ms -- six a second -- and variant A
16081               	; 	' copies both. Ten a second was tried on the way here and reads as
16082               	; 	' hurrying rather than running. What D changes is not the cadence but the
16083               	; 	' TICK: two frames rather than four, and a notch louder to carry at half
16084               	; 	' the length. Same six a second, less of it.
16085               	; 	'
16086               	; 	' EIGHT A SECOND, AND THE ACCUMULATOR NOW CARRIES ITS REMAINDER.
16087               	; 	'
16088               	; 	' sfw counted pixels and the trigger did `sfw = 0`, THROWING AWAY whatever
16089               	; 	' was past the threshold. kspd is about four pixels a pass, so a threshold
16090               	; 	' of 17 did not fire at 17 -- it fired at the first multiple past it, about
16091               	; 	' 20, and every rate this was ever set to came out slower than the number
16092               	; 	' said: the "six a second" was 5.2 and the "ten" that read as hurrying was
16093               	; 	' really 8.7. Subtracting the threshold instead keeps the fraction, so the
16094               	; 	' rate is what it claims to be at any walking speed.
16095               	; 	'
16096               	; 	' MEASURED OFF THE COLECOVISION: 14 px, about 7.4 a second.
16097               	; 	'
16098               	; 	' It was 15 px and 6.9 a second, picked between an 8.0 that read as
16099               	; 	' slightly hurried and a 6.1 that read as trudging -- a judgement between
16100               	; 	' two other judgements, with nothing underneath it. The ColecoVision
16101               	; 	' recording settles it: footfalls land every 0.130 s across a twelve-second
16102               	; 	' continuous run, which is 7.7 a second, and that is the one finding in the
16103               	; 	' whole sound analysis the method resolves EXACTLY -- a rhythm rather than a
16104               	; 	' pitch, counted off the RMS track rather than inferred from a spectrum.
16105               	; 	' (colecosounds variant 1A; assets/sfx/sfxref-coleco.md has the working.)
16106               	; 	'
16107               	; 	' 104 px/s over 14 px is 7.43 a second. 13 px would give 8.00, and 7.7 sits
16108               	; 	' almost exactly between them -- so this is the nearer of the two, and it is
16109               	; 	' also the one that does not walk back into the 8.0 that was rejected by ear.
16110               	; 	'
16111               	; 	' WHY THE GAME KEEPS A DISTANCE AND THE BENCH KEEPS A CADENCE. The bench
16112               	; 	' plays a fixed eight frames between steps because it has no walking to tie
16113               	; 	' them to; the game accumulates PIXELS TRAVELLED, so the feet keep time with
16114               	; 	' the legs when he is slowed or stopped. Matching "7.4 a second" therefore
16115               	; 	' means matching it AT HIS WALKING SPEED, and assumes the ColecoVision's
16116               	; 	' crook walks at ours -- which the recording cannot confirm.
16117               	; 	'
16118               	; 	' The dial is this one constant and the subtraction below, which must stay
16119               	; 	' threshold + 1 or the carry is wrong.
16120               	; 	'
16121               	; 	' SOT = 2 IS THE SHORTEST TICK THERE IS, and 1 is SILENCE. The decay block
16122               	; 	' below runs LATER IN THE SAME sfx_tick, so a count of 1 is decremented to
16123               	; 	' zero on the pass that set it and the note-off fires before the sound has
16124               	; 	' lasted any time at all. 2 survives to the next pass, which is one pass of
16125               	; 	' sound -- about 42 ms against the bench's 33, as close as a per-pass timer
16126               	; 	' gets, and the reason the bench and the game cannot sound identical.
16127               	; 	'
16128               	; 	' Register 4 is white noise at the fastest rate.
16129               	; 	'
16130               	; 	' VOLUME 9, WHICH IS UNDER EVERYTHING ELSE ON PURPOSE. The hit, the prize

16334 F57E 0450  20 	b *r0
16335               	;
16336               	; 	' EVERYTHING BELOW THIS LINE IS ASSEMBLED INTO BANK 1, so the INCLUDE order
16337               	; 	' is load-bearing and nothing but data may follow it.
16338               	; 	'
16339               	; 	' THE FONT IS NOW IN THE BANK TOO, and it used to be deliberately outside:
16340               	; 	' keeping one readable thing in bank 0 means a bank-selection mistake shows
16341               	; 	' as "text survives, art does not" rather than a uniformly blank screen,
16342               	; 	' which is a genuinely useful thing to have when a bank goes wrong.
16343               	; 	'
16344               	; 	' THE FONT HAS A BANK OF ITS OWN, and the reason is not its size.
16345               	; 	'
16346               	; 	' Bank 1 was FULL -- six spare bytes of 8,192 -- which shut the door on
16347               	; 	' moving anything else out of the fixed area, and the fixed area is the
16348               	; 	' only budget that cannot be grown (linkticart writes exactly three
16349               	; 	' loader pages and discards the rest; they are the 32K expansion's RAM at
16350               	; 	' >A000, not cart ROM). A second bank costs a bigger cart -- five pages
16351               	; 	' round up to eight, so 32 KB becomes 64 KB -- and buys back the ability
16352               	; 	' to keep evacuating data out of code.
16353               	; 	'
16354               	; 	' THE FONT IS THE RIGHT TENANT because it is read ONCE. Two DEFINEs copy
16355               	; 	' it into VRAM at setup and nothing looks at it again, so it is the only
16356               	; 	' block here that can sit on a page which is not permanently mapped. See
16357               	; 	' setup_font: bank 2 is selected for those two statements and bank 1 for
16358               	; 	' the whole of the rest of the program.
16359               	; 	'
16360               	; 	' EVERYTHING ELSE STAYS IN BANK 1, because everything else is read during
16361               	; 	' play -- art on a screen crossing, templates on a band blit, the lookup
16362               	; 	' tables every pass. One permanently-mapped bank for all of it means
16363               	; 	' there is no switch to miss.
16364               	; 	#if TI994A
16365               	; 	BANK 2
16366      0A7E     BANK_0_FREE:	EQU >fffe-$
     **** ****     > .rept

16504               	;
16505               	; 	' THE COLOUR TABLE, 472 bytes of the same value ($B4 = black ink on dark blue).
16506               	; 	'
16507               	; 	' Loaded with DEFINE COLOR 32,59,font_col, which is ONE synchronous call that
16508               	; 	' writes all three screen thirds (define_color always does the LDIRVM3 triple
16509               	; 	' copy). It replaced a VPOKE loop that wrote this one value 1,416 times paced by
16510               	; 	' 24 WAITs -- the largest scripted delay in the boot, and the reason the title
16511               	; 	' screen used to fill in visibly rather than appearing at once.
16512               	; 	'
16513               	; 	' EIGHT BYTES PER CHARACTER, not one. Supply fewer and DEFINE COLOR reads
16514               	; 	' whatever follows in ROM as colour data, with no error at build or run time.
16515               	;
16516               	; font_col:
16517               cvb_FONT_COL

17180               	; 	INCLUDE "art.bas"
17181               	; 	' Keystone Kapers art -- GENERATED by assets/genart.py. Do not edit; regenerate.
17182               	; 	'
17183               	; 	' EVERY SPRITE IS 16x16: sprite size and magnification are GLOBAL on the
17184               	; 	' TMS9918, so small objects are drawn small INSIDE a 16x16 box rather than
17185               	; 	' being small sprites.
17186               	; 	'
17187               	; 	' EVERY 8-PX OBJECT SITS IN ROWS 8-15 OF ITS BOX, ducked Kelly included, so
17188               	; 	' one rule places them all: bottom edge = y + 16, and a thing resting on the
17189               	; 	' floor is at y = FLOORY - 16.
17190               	; 	'
17191               	; 	' Sprite bytes are QUADRANT-ORDERED: 16 rows of the left half, then 16 of
17192               	; 	' the right. Every block is an EVEN number of bytes -- an odd DATA BYTE run
17193               	; 	' silently misaligns every word table after it (CLAUDE.md 3A).
17194               	;
17195               	; spr_kelly:	' Kelly: RIGHT hat/face/two merged run bodies/two FREE slots/duck hat/face/body, then the same LEFT (+36). The run bodies carry tunic AND legs, so a frame is one sprite, and standing is run frame 1. Patterns 0..68

18427               	; 	INCLUDE "store.bas"
18428               	; 	' Keystone Kapers store -- GENERATED by assets/genstore.py. Do not edit.
18429               	; 	'
18430               	; 	' EIGHT band templates of 5 rows x 32 cols (160 bytes each) plus a 32-byte
18431               	; 	' index over (level, screen). The whole 8-screen, 4-level building is about
18432               	; 	' 1.3 KB instead of the 5,120 bytes it would cost to store literally.
18433               	; 	'
18434               	; 	' All eight templates are ONE contiguous block under ONE label, so a band
18435               	; 	' blit is
18436               	; 	'     SCREEN stor_tpl, tpl*160, toprow*32, 32, 5, 32
18437               	; 	' with no label ladder -- SCREEN needs a literal label and a label cannot be
18438               	; 	' chosen by a variable, which is why RallyX needed a 4-way IF over its maze
18439               	; 	' tables. One block sidesteps it.
18440               	; 	'
18441               	; 	' 160 is EVEN, so this cannot leave the location counter odd and misalign
18442               	; 	' the word tables defined after it.
18443               	; 	'
18444               	; 	' template ids:
18445               	; 	'   0 T_AISLE_A
18446               	; 	'   1 T_AISLE_B
18447               	; 	'   2 T_ESC_W
18448               	; 	'   3 T_ESC_E
18449               	; 	'   4 T_ELEV
18450               	; 	'   5 T_ROOF0
18451               	; 	'   6 T_ROOF1
18452               	; 	'   7 T_ROOF2

19077               	;
19078               	; 	' THE SKYLINE'S LAST BAND WITHOUT ITS YELLOW, high nibble ink, low nibble
19079               	; 	' paper, one byte a scan line -- the same shape genart emits into
19080               	; 	' store_col. SKY2 is white-on-9 throughout instead of turning to paper 10
19081               	; 	' at row 4; BLDGL holds its blue one row longer and then meets its own
19082               	; 	' grey wall. Both are the generated bytes with 10 replaced by 9 and
19083               	; 	' nothing else changed. See setup_rest.
19084               	; #if NES
19085               	; nes_sky2c:
19086               	; 	DATA BYTE $F9,$F9,$F9,$F9,$F9,$F9,$F9,$F9
19087               	; nes_bldlc:
19088               	; 	DATA BYTE $B9,$B9,$B9,$B9,$B9,$BE,$BE,$BE
19089               	; #endif
19090               	;
19091               	; 	' THE IN-GAME FONT'S COLOUR, one byte a scan line and eight a character for
19092               	; 	' all 59 of them. $B4 is light yellow on dark blue -- ink index 3, paper index 1 --
19093               	; 	' and which colours those are is then the attribute table's business, per
19094               	; 	' region: dark blue behind the HUD, the store's green behind a message box.
19095               	; 	'
19096               	; 	' 472 bytes of one repeated value. That reads like waste and is the cheap
19097               	; 	' option: ROM is three budgets here and this is not the scarce one, while
19098               	; 	' the alternative is a second font (impossible -- only eleven free codes)
19099               	; 	' or a new uploader parameter (no RAM -- two bytes left).
